title: Design Patterns: What, Why, and the GoF Categories
summary: What a design pattern really is, the three GoF categories, and why reaching for one too eagerly can hurt more than plain code.

slides.markdown: A **design pattern** is a named, reusable shape for solving a recurring design problem — not a library, not a language feature, just a proven arrangement of objects and responsibilities. The Gang of Four (GoF) catalog groups patterns into three families: **creational** (how objects get built), **structural** (how objects fit together), and **behavioral** (how objects communicate). Think of a pattern like a recipe name — it lets two engineers agree on a shape without re-explaining every step.

slides.sectionTitle: What a design pattern actually is
slides.markdown:
A pattern is not a class you import — it's a **shape**: a named arrangement of roles (like "creator" and "product") that recurs across unrelated codebases. You still write the code yourself, adapted to your language and problem.

This matters because copying a pattern's textbook example verbatim usually produces awkward, over-engineered code — the value is in recognizing the *shape* of your problem, then choosing (or not choosing) a matching arrangement.

For example, "Observer" is a shape (subject notifies registered listeners) — it looks completely different in a Java `Observable` class, a JavaScript `EventEmitter`, and a React dependency array, yet all three are the same pattern underneath.

Takeaway: learn patterns as vocabulary for shapes, not as boilerplate to paste.

The Gang of Four's 1994 catalog splits 23 patterns into three questions a design has to answer. **Creational** patterns answer "how does this object get built?" (Factory Method, Builder, Singleton, Prototype, Abstract Factory). **Structural** patterns answer "how do these objects compose into larger structures?" (Adapter, Decorator, Facade). **Behavioral** patterns answer "how do these objects talk to each other and share responsibility?" (Strategy, Observer, Command).

Knowing which bucket a pattern lives in tells you what kind of problem it solves before you've even learned its details — if your pain is "too many constructor overloads," you're in creational territory, not behavioral.

This group covers the five creational patterns in depth.

slides.markdown:
![Three columns — Creational, Structural, Behavioral — with Creational's five patterns listed](assets/gof-families.svg)

The 23 GoF patterns split unevenly: five creational, seven structural, eleven behavioral. Creational patterns are the smallest family but the one nearly every codebase touches early, since every object has to get constructed somehow.

This group works through all five creational patterns in the order most interview prep guides teach them: two factory variants, then Builder, Singleton, and Prototype.

slides.markdown:
Patterns exist to give engineers a **shared vocabulary** for design conversations, not to make code fancier. Saying "let's use a Factory here" in a design review communicates an entire arrangement of classes in three words — the alternative is drawing the class diagram from scratch every time.

That compression is the entire value proposition. A pattern name that isn't shared knowledge on your team is worse than useless — it hides the design behind jargon instead of revealing it.

Takeaway: a pattern's job is to save communication, not to save typing.

**Wrong belief:** "This is a real design problem, so I should use a named pattern to solve it properly."

**Why it's wrong:** patterns solve *specific* recurring shapes — forcing one where the problem doesn't need that flexibility adds classes, indirection, and cognitive load for a benefit nobody will ever use. A single `if/else` choosing between two report formats doesn't need a Strategy interface and two implementing classes.

**Correct model:** reach for a pattern only when you can name the actual variability it buys you — a real axis that changes at runtime or across deployments. If you can't name that axis, plain code is the better design.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: pattern vs idiom vs framework
slides.markdown:
**Pattern**, **idiom**, and **framework** solve design problems at different altitudes, and interviewers use the words loosely enough that mixing them up is a common stumble.

| | Scope | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Idiom | A language-specific trick | Python's `with` for resource cleanup |
| Pattern | A language-agnostic arrangement of roles | Factory Method, Observer |
| Framework | A reusable, opinionated skeleton you plug code into | Spring, Django, React |

**How to decide:** if the solution only makes sense in one language, it's an idiom; if it's an arrangement you could redraw as a class diagram in any OO language, it's a pattern; if it calls your code instead of the other way around, it's a framework.

Interviewers rarely ask you to recite the GoF definition of Singleton — they ask **"have you used this, and why?"** because reciting a definition proves memorization, not judgment.

The strong answer names a real system: "I used a Builder for a payment-request object with nine optional fields, because telescoping constructors were producing call sites nobody could read." The weak answer restates the textbook definition with no context.

Prepare one concrete, specific story per pattern — the problem it solved, not just what the pattern does — and you'll clear this bar in almost any interview.
